fun_facts: A nest's sand temperature decides the hatchlings' sex, not their genes: a few degrees above roughly 29°C and a nest hatches mostly female, a few degrees below and it hatches mostly male.

A nesting female almost always comes ashore on the same short stretch of beach where she herself hatched decades earlier, guided in part by a faint magnetic signature of that coastline she imprinted on as a hatchling.

After hatching, loggerheads vanish into the open Atlantic for close to a decade, often drifting inside mats of Sargassum weed as far as the Azores, before turning up again in coastal waters as juveniles -- a stretch researchers call "the lost years" because so little of it was ever directly observed.

measures.label: Curved carapace length
measures.help: Measured with a flexible tape along the curve of the shell, from the nuchal notch to the longer posterior tip.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: Sex cannot be told by looking at a turtle in the field, nesting females aside; unknown is the normal answer for anything but a nesting encounter.

not_taggable.reason: flipper tags in this programme are applied to nesting adult females on the beach; a turtle this small is a juvenile encountered elsewhere and is not part of that protocol

must_release.reason: loggerhead sea turtles are federally protected under the Endangered Species Act; every animal encountered must be released, regardless of size
